title: "Head Down, Fist on Head" for Answering Diagnostic Questions
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton names the recurring flaw of multiple-choice diagnostic questions as the 'tactical delay' — the pause where a student peeks at a reliably correct classmate's answer before committing to their own. Drawing on a conversation with Science teacher Pritesh Raichura, he describes a technique borrowed from Dani Quinn called 'Heads Down, Fist on Head': students rest their heads on the desk with their eyes covered, hold up a closed fist, and open it only when the teacher calls their chosen letter option, so no one can see anyone else's answer. The teacher then tallies open fists option by option and can call on individual students afterward to explain their reasoning. Barton lists four benefits: it removes the incentive for tactical delay or clamming up, needs no equipment, reduces information overload for the teacher compared with 30 simultaneous whiteboards, and is quieter than a show-of-hands method.
points: Barton names the core validity problem with multiple-choice diagnostic questions as the 'tactical delay' — students glancing at a reliable peer's answer before revealing their own.

The 'Heads Down, Fist on Head' technique, borrowed via Pritesh Raichura from Dani Quinn, has students hide their eyes and reveal only a closed or open fist per answer option, eliminating the chance to see classmates' choices.
He argues the technique also solves an information-overload problem for the teacher, since watching fists open option-by-option is easier to track trends from than 30 simultaneous mini-whiteboards.
A secondary benefit noted is stealth: opening a fist is silent, whereas raising a hand to indicate a choice can trigger giveaway rustling from neighbors.
quotes: But diagnostic questions have an inherent problem: the tactical delay . This is when the teacher says: show me your choice of answer in 3, 2, 1, go… and some students pause for a second or two whilst they have a cheeky look at the answers of students who are usually correct.

They then either have their choice of answer confirmed, or engage in an impressive sleight of hand whilst their C magically becomes an A. This reduces the validity of the check for understanding, or can cause students to clam up when they realise their choice of answer is the minority.
Students place their left-arm on the desk and rest their head upon it so they cannot see their classmates
The teacher observes the number of open fists (and makes a note of student names if their memory is as bad as mine)
Students cannot see other answers, so there is no incentive to engage in a tactical delay or clam up when asked for their explanation
It reduces the flow of information (as opposed to 30 students showing you their answers at once), so you are more likely to be able to identify trends
The opening of the first is pretty silent, whereas asking students to raise their hand to indicate their choice may result in a give-away rustling
